title: Brazil graft scandal billionaire Odebrecht moved to house arrest
text: Marcelo Odebrecht, the billionaire who was the highest-profile executive jailed in Brazil's sprawling graft scandal, left prison on Tuesday to serve the remainder of his corruption sentence under house arrest, a federal court said. Odebrecht, the former chief executive of Odebrecht SA, Latin America's largest construction company, was arrested in 2015 in the investigation known as Car Wash, which uncovered billions of dollars in kickbacks paid to politicians and to executives at state-run companies in return for inflated contracts. According to the federal court in Parana, he was due to travel to Sao Paulo on Tuesday to start his house arrest under electronic monitoring. A representative for Odebrecht said he remained committed to cooperating with authorities under a leniency deal. In one of the many Car Wash cases, Odebrecht was initially sentenced to 19 years in prison. The term was cut to 10 years after he signed a leniency agreement last December, under which he agreed to pay a fine of nearly $2 billion, admit guilt and give evidence to authorities. He has already spent two-and-a-half years in prison. The deal requires him to spend another two-and-a-half years under house arrest, after which he will be allowed to leave home to work for a further two-and-a-half years. He must then perform community service for the remainder of his 10-year sentence. Also on Tuesday, Brazil's antitrust watchdog Cade said it was looking into two alleged cartels involved in bidding for Sao Paulo infrastructure projects after receiving information from Odebrecht executives.

title: Chris Paul's quick hands and gruesome fingers
text: Chris Paul looked over his crooked knuckles and the surgical scars that trace tiny road maps across his hands. He has torn various ligaments in his thumbs and broken bones in his fingers, and he has worn casts and splints. Yet however gruesome they look, his hands are the indispensable tools of his trade. “I’ve got the worst fingers,” he said. Paul, the starting point guard for the Los Angeles Clippers, long ago established himself as one of the NBA's premier defenders. No other active player in the league has collected more steals: 1,892 and counting. He clutters passing lanes. He strips dribbles like paint thinner. His coach, Doc Rivers, has concluded that Paul has the best hands he has ever seen. “Gifted,” Rivers said during an interview in January. “His hands are so damn quick.” Three days after Rivers made that assessment, Paul paid the price for having such gifts. Fighting through a screen in a game against the Oklahoma City Thunder, he jammed his left thumb and tore his ulnar collateral ligament, which is not to be confused with his radial collateral ligament, the one he tore in his right thumb while training for the Olympics in 2012. Few people on the planet know firsthand the difference between RCL and UCL tears. Paul is one of them. (Both hurt, he said.) After his most recent injury, Paul missed 14 games before returning late last month. Even now, as the Clippers compete for playoff position, he is trying to regain his feel for the game. “I see plays all the time where I know I can reach for the ball and I know I can steal it,” he said.

title: The Truth About Hillary Clinton's Record On LGBT Rights
text: Hillary Clinton is a complicated woman running in a country that wants its political platforms to fit on a trucker's cap. As a candidate, she has taken plenty of heat from progressives for coming around late on marriage equality. She did, but it's not that simple. Scratch just a little below the surface and you'll find a true champion of LGBT rights all over the world. There are plenty of legitimate complaints about Clinton's evolution on LGBT rights. First, her husband's legacy, which also isn't that simple, is the failed military policy of Don't Ask, Don't Tell. Bill Clinton didn't love the policy, but he saw it as the best compromise at the time. Of course, that wasn't Hillary's policy. In fact, back in 1999 she said she was against Don't Ask, Don't Tell, so let's move on. The criticism with the most teeth is that Hillary didn't come around to accepting marriage equality until just three years ago, but that was only one step in a long history of support. One accomplishment that has gotten scant attention is that she ushered gay rights onto the international stage. It is fair to say that without Clinton's efforts, the global struggle for equality for gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender (LGBT) people would not have moved as fast as it has over the past several years, nor would the United States be seen today as a global leader in that struggle. At the heart of those efforts was the 2011 United Nations Human Rights Council Resolution on Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity, otherwise known as the UNHRC Gay Rights Resolution, an international agreement whose drafting and signing Clinton oversaw.

title: Trump worker-contract case raises conflict-of-interest question
text: U.S. President-elect Donald Trump has frequently boasted about the strict confidentiality pledges he requires of his employees. Now a legal challenge to one of those agreements is pending before a U.S. agency over which he will soon have influence, potentially posing an early test of concerns about conflicts of interest between Trump's public role and his business empire. In September, a worker-advocacy group filed a charge with the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) claiming that a nondisclosure contract used by Trump is unlawfully broad. The contract bars employees, independent contractors and even volunteers from ever disclosing any information that Trump deems confidential about his personal, business or political life. The NLRB has said that sweeping or unclear contracts inhibit workers from discussing working conditions or talking to union organizers. The five-member NLRB currently has two vacancies that Trump is slated to fill early in his term, likely shifting an agency that has leaned liberal under President Barack Obama toward a more business-friendly posture. A ruling against Trump by the NLRB could free workers to speak more openly about their concerns and strengthen their bargaining power. Besides the confidentiality case, about 10 other Trump-related cases are pending at the NLRB. Those cases involve alleged labor violations at the Trump International Hotel Las Vegas, where management has refused to bargain with the Culinary Workers Union. It was not clear whether the confidentiality contract was meant for workers on Trump's election campaign or for employees in his businesses, and its authenticity could not be independently verified. Representatives of the Trump Organization did not respond to requests for comment. The case is at a very early stage and could be settled or dismissed before it reaches a full hearing before the five-member NLRB.

title: Apple's new MacBook Pro: fast and light, but not for everyone
text: When Apple unveiled its new MacBook Pro laptops at a media event last month, software engineer Adam Leventhal was keen to learn about them. But by the time he had finished watching a live stream of the event, Mr. Leventhal, who has owned only Mac computers for the last 30 years, had been turned off. “With this one I was really disappointed,” he said. As new laptops go, the MacBook Pro has been divisive. That may be partly because the model, long used by creative professionals and coders, has stayed largely unchanged since 2012. So when Apple introduced some fairly radical changes this time, emotions ran high among some longtime Mac customers. In their latest form, MacBook Pros have just one type of connection port, rather than the several types they had before, which means people will need to buy adapters to plug in devices that use other kinds of connectors. Apple also replaced the top row of physical keys on the keyboard, including the Escape key, with a virtual touch strip called the Touch Bar. The benefits? The new laptops are faster, much thinner and lighter than the previous generation, and they get about 10 hours of battery life. The Touch Bar's virtual buttons change depending on the app you are using, opening up the potential for software makers to create custom shortcuts. I tested the new MacBook Pros, which cost $1,500 to $2,800 depending on the model, while collecting reactions to the new computers from engineers and information technology professionals over two weeks. My conclusion: while the new laptops are capable enough for many professionals, there is no need to rush out and buy one.

title: Kenya university siege ends with 147 dead
text: Armed terrorists stormed a university in northern Kenya on Thursday, killing 147 people, wounding dozens and taking hostages in a 15-hour siege that ended when security forces killed four militants. The targets appeared to be Christians and converts to Islam. More than 550 students were evacuated and 79 were injured in the standoff at the Garissa University campus, about 90 miles from the Somali border. The Somalia-based Islamic terrorist group al-Shabab claimed responsibility for the attack, the deadliest in Kenya by the al-Qaeda-linked organization. Students said the gunmen separated Christians from Muslims and held hostages in a dormitory, where they placed explosives around the Christian hostages, according to Kenya's National Police Service. Kenyan Interior Cabinet Secretary Joseph Nkaissery said some students were killed during morning prayers at the mosque. Police Inspector General Joseph Boinett said a dusk-to-dawn curfew will be imposed in Garissa and three neighboring counties from Friday through April 16. The White House strongly condemned the attack and said the United States was providing assistance to the Kenyan government.

title: Federal judge blocks Indiana abortion law
text: A federal judge on Thursday blocked an Indiana law that would have banned abortions based solely on a fetus's disability or genetic anomaly, suggesting that it was an illegal limit on a woman's constitutional right. Judge Tanya Walton Pratt of the Federal District Court for Southern Indiana also held up a state ban on abortions motivated solely by a fetus's race or sex. In the preliminary injunction, Judge Pratt said that limiting the reasons for an abortion was “inconsistent with the notion of a right rooted in privacy concerns and a liberty right to make independent decisions.” Although Judge Pratt's injunction prevents the law from taking immediate effect, and although she said the state would be unlikely to prevail at trial, the state can still defend the legislation. In a statement, the Indiana attorney general's office said state lawyers would consider how to proceed and whether to appeal the injunction. Indiana would have been the first state with a blanket ban on abortions based solely on race, sex or suspected disabilities, including evidence of Down syndrome. A handful of states ban abortion based on sex, one state bans it based on race, and two ban it based on genetic anomalies, according to the Guttmacher Institute, a nonprofit abortion rights group that tracks state laws. Judge Pratt's decision, the first in a federal court to indicate that a ban on abortion because of genetic anomalies would likely be unconstitutional, is the latest setback for such groups. It comes days after a landmark Supreme Court ruling in a Texas case that two other kinds of restrictions, requiring doctors who perform abortions to have admitting privileges at local hospitals and imposing stringent standards on abortion clinics, are unconstitutional. The Texas measures would have forced many clinics to close.

title: Michael Flynn resigns as national security adviser
text: Michael T. Flynn, the national security adviser, resigned on Monday night after it emerged that he had misled Vice President Mike Pence and other senior White House officials about his conversations with the Russian ambassador to the United States. title: With Trump leaving a legislative void, Republicans slow to take on big issues
text: Nearly a month into his presidency, Donald Trump has yet to unveil major legislation or publicly back bills from others, giving Republicans a slow start on the sweeping reforms they promised on the campaign trail. As Trump and Republicans lurch from crisis to crisis, lawmakers have scaled back expectations for legislative action in 2017 on tax reform, health care, financial regulation, jobs and infrastructure, and some are calling for more guidance from the White House. Trump has offered few specifics on such issues in his more than two dozen executive orders, proclamations and memoranda. A temporary ban on U.S. entry by refugees and people from seven Muslim-majority countries was blocked in court. Trump's ambitious campaign promises helped Republicans sweep the White House, the Senate and the House of Representatives in November's national elections. Legislation could start moving soon now that the Senate has confirmed nine of Trump's Cabinet nominees and is poised to approve others shortly, despite delays by Democrats. But concern is growing among some Republicans and moderate Democrats who had hoped for more by this point. On taxes, for example, Republican Senator Lindsey Graham said in an interview, “What I’d like to see the administration do is lead on this issue.” The White House needs to “either come out with their own tax cut plan or weigh in pretty quickly,” he said. “I’m getting unnerved that there’s lack of coordination.” Last week, Trump promised a “phenomenal” tax plan within weeks but gave no details. Nor has he firmly endorsed or opposed the tax reform proposals under debate in Congress. At a party retreat last month, lawmakers welcomed remarks by Trump that appeared to support a House Republican “border adjustment” tax designed to encourage exports and discourage imports.
